results.title: Opera Game, after 9… b5
results.question: Explain the idea behind Stockfish's best move in this position.
results.answer:
10. Nxb5 [+4.47] is about four and a half pawns better for White, so the idea is to cash in on Black's 9...b5 error while keeping the initiative.

The knight takes a pawn that Black's c6-pawn was guarding, and it's defended by the queen on b3, so Black can't simply win it back. The bigger point is what follows. After 10...a6 kicks the knight, 11. Bxf6 attacks Black's queen on e7 and removes a defender of Black's position. Black has to find a counter-attack such as 11...Qb4+, and the engine line continues 12. c3 Qxb3, which trades queens with White still ahead.

Black's king is still in the centre, and White's pieces are already developed and pointing at it. That combination of material and activity is the same theme as Morphy's Opera Game, where development matters more than keeping every pawn.

For the general principles behind moves like this, the chapter on open games (the Philidor family) in *Fundamental Chess Openings* by Paul van der Sterren explains the typical plans.

results.title: 1. e4 e5 2. Qh5 Nc6 3. Bc4: Black to move
results.question: Is there a tactic in the air for either side right now? What should I watch for?
results.answer:
Yes, White has a real threat: 4. Qxf7 is checkmate. The bishop on c4 defends f7, the king on e8 has no escape (d8 and f8 are occupied, and the queen covers e7). Black has to address this now.

The engine's top choice, 3…g6 [−0.25, a little better for Black], kicks the queen. Stockfish's main line is 4. Qf3 Nf6 5. Ne2 Bg7 6. d3 d6 7. Nbc3.

Two other defences are in the engine lines:

- 3…Qe7 [−0.14]: the queen guards f7 and keeps the kingside closed. Stockfish gives 4. Qd1 Qh4 5. Nc3 Bc5 6. Qf3 f5 7. g3.

- 3…Nh6 [+0.25, slightly better for White]: the knight guards f7, but White keeps the initiative. Stockfish gives 4. d3 g6 5. Qg5 f6 6. Qh4 Nf7 7. f4.

The practical lesson: when the opponent's queen eyes a pawn next to an uncastled king, check first whether it is mate. Any move that doesn't cover f7 or move the king loses at once. Moves such as 3…Nf6 are not in the engine lines, so treat them as unchecked.

For the ideas behind these lines, read the chapter on this opening family in *Fundamental Chess Openings* by Paul van der Sterren. *Logical Chess: Move by Move* by Irving Chernev explains similar attacking moves in full.

results.title: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Nd4 4. Nxe5: Black to move
results.question: Is there a tactic in the air for either side right now? What should I watch for?
results.answer:
Yes, both sides have immediate tactics, and the loose knights on e5 and d4 are the reason.

Black is to move, and the engine's best try is 4...Qg5 (about half a pawn better for Black [-0.51]). The queen attacks the unprotected ~~Ne5~~ along the fifth rank, and White's natural answer is 5. Bxf7+ Kd8 6. Ng4, when the king and the knight on g4 both need care. The engine also shows that grabbing with 4...Qe7 is not enough: after 5. Nxf7 Qxe4+, White is still about a pawn better [+0.86], because the knight's escape comes with tempo.

For White, the main danger is the bishop on c4 combining with the knight on e5 against f7. If Black lets the knight move without a plan, Bxf7+ can hit the king and win material. Black's own Nd4 is also loose, but 4...Nxc2+ is not in the engine lines, so treat it as unchecked. Qxc2 wins the knight back, so don't rely on it.

Watch for the king in the centre and the open e-file. Both sides' queens and loose pieces are the targets. Ideas like this come up in Chernev's *Logical Chess: Move by Move*, which explains why such captures and checks work in master games.

results.title: Queen's Gambit: the Elephant Trap after 6. Nxd5
results.question: Is there a tactic in the air for either side right now? What should I watch for?
results.answer:
Yes. Black to move can win material immediately with 6...Nxd5. White's knight on d5 is undefended, so Black simply captures it.

The knight on f6 is also blocking the bishop on g5, which attacks the queen on d8. Once Nxd5 moves that knight, the bishop can take the queen, so White has a counterpunch, but it doesn't save White. The engine line is:

- 6...Nxd5 7. Bxd8 Bb4+ 8. Qd2 Bxd2+ 9. Kxd2 Kxd8 10. e4 (about five pawns better for Black [-4.77])

Watch for these ideas:
- For Black: Nxd5 wins the knight and opens the diagonal. Don't be distracted by the queen trade that follows, since the engine still sees Black far ahead.
- For White: Bxd8 grabs the queen, but Bb4+ forces the queen trade, and Black's king recaptures the bishop.
- Engine's suggestion for White: e3 at +0.40 was better than 6. Nxd5 and keeps the position roughly level.

For general tactical thinking, *Logical Chess: Move by Move* by Irving Chernev explains why moves like these work, one move at a time.

results.title: A back-rank mate in one
results.question: Explain the idea behind Stockfish's best move in this position.
results.answer:
1. Ra8# is checkmate, and it works because Black's own pawns trap the king.

The rook on a1 slides up the open a-file to a8, giving check along the eighth rank. Black's king on g8 has no flight squares: f8 and h8 are covered by the rook, and f7, g7 and h7 are blocked by Black's own pawns. Black also has no piece that can step between the rook and the king. That's a back-rank mate.

The idea to take away is to look for an open back rank whenever the enemy king is boxed in by its own pawns. Here Black's last move left that pattern in place, so the rook check ends the game. White's rook being loose on a1 doesn't matter, because Black never gets a move.

For a classic example of this pattern in a richer setting, look at Morphy's Opera Game from the built-in collection, where the back-rank theme comes up in an attack.

results.title: Steinitz–von Bardeleben, before 17. d5
results.question: What is the main plan for the side to move here, and why?
results.answer:
White's best plan is the central break 17. d5!, which the engine rates as clearly best, about two pawns better for White [+1.91]. White's isolated d-pawn is a weakness normally, but here pushing it at the right moment turns it into a lever. After 17...cxd5 18. Nd4 Kf7 19. Ne6 Nc6 20. Nc5 Qd6, White's knight reaches strong squares while Black's queen gets pushed around.

The idea is to open lines before Black untangles. The c-file and e-file are opening, and White's rooks on c1 and e1 are ready to use them. Black's king is still on e8 with castling rights, so open files and active White pieces make it hard to get safe. Black's rooks on a8 and h8 are also undefended, which gives White tactical chances.

Slower options are weaker. 17. Nd2 [+0.52] regroups toward e4 and c5, and 17. Qc4 [+0.43] is playable, but both leave the pawn tension unresolved.

For the plan, read the Isolated Queen Pawn chapter of *Chess Structures* by Mauricio Flores Rios. For a model of this exact idea, study Steinitz vs Bardeleben (Hastings 1895) in the built-in collection, and the similar position from your library.

results.title: King and pawn: Black has the opposition
results.question: What is the main plan for the side to move here, and why?
results.answer:
White's plan is to centralise the king and use it to escort the e-pawn, pushing e4 only when the king can support it. Black's king is the defender here, so the pawn can't advance alone.

Stockfish prefers 1. Kf3 [+0.12], which is essentially equal with a tiny edge for White. After 1...Kf5 2. Ke3 Ke5 3. Kd3 Kd5 4. e4+ Ke6, the pawn advances with check and the king on d3 backs it up. Black keeps matching each king move, so White must make progress with the king rather than hurry the pawn.

Also note 1. Kd3 Kd5 2. e4+ Ke6 [+0.11], which reaches the same setup a move faster. The key idea is that the pawn needs its king beside it before it moves.

For this, Dvoretsky's Endgame Manual and the king and pawn chapters of 100 Endgames You Must Know by Jesús de la Villa cover these key positions. The classic study «Réti's king march» shows how an active king can support its own pawn and attack the enemy one at the same time.

results.title: The Lucena position
results.question: Explain the idea behind Stockfish's best move in this position.
results.answer:
Stockfish's favourite, 1. Rd1+, is about four and a half pawns better for White [+4.60]. The idea is to drive the black king away from the queenside, where it could defend the b-pawn, and then keep it out.

After 1…Ke6 2. Rd4, the rook cuts the king off along the fourth rank. Black's only counterplay is the rook, which checks from behind with 2…Rb2. White then steps the king off the eighth rank with 3. Ka7, clearing the path for the pawn. The pawn and the cutting rook do the work, and Black's rook is left to make harmless checks.

Note that the quiet 1. Rb1 is almost as good [+4.58], so the check is not the only route. The lesson is the plan: push the enemy king away, cut it off, and let the pawn advance.

For the technique, look at the rook-and-pawn-versus-rook chapter in *100 Endgames You Must Know* by Jesús de la Villa, which covers the Lucena and Philidor positions. The Lucena game in the built-in collection shows the same bridge idea.

results.title: The Philidor position: Black to move
results.question: What is the main plan for the side to move here, and why?
results.answer:
Black is the defending side, so the plan is to keep the rook active on the sixth rank and hold the e-pawn. This is the Philidor idea: the rook stops White's king from getting in front of the pawn, and Black can check from behind when needed.

- 1...Rb6 is the clearest version. The rook stays on the sixth rank, and after 2.Rc7 Rh6 Black keeps a rook ready to meet White's rook.

- 1...Ra2 is the alternative. The rook works from behind, and after 2.Ke6 Ra6+ 3.Kf5 Rb6, it returns to the sixth rank with a check first.

- All three top moves score between +0.10 and +0.13 for White, about a tenth of a pawn. That is effectively level, so Black is holding, not losing.

Black's rook on a6 is loose, and White's rook on h7 is loose too, so tactics matter. In the engine line 2.Rc7 Rh6 3.Rc6 Rxc6 4.Kxc6 Ke7 5.Kd5, the rooks come off and the game becomes a king-and-pawn ending that the engine still rates as level.

For study, the rook-and-pawn-versus-rook section of *100 Endgames You Must Know* by Jesús de la Villa covers the Philidor setup, and the built-in Philidor game (1777) shows the defensive technique in action.

results.title: Sicilian after 3. d4
results.question: What is the main plan for the side to move here, and why?
results.answer:
Black's main plan is to develop and challenge the centre without giving White an easy target. The best move, 3...Nf6 [−0.29 for Black, so White is about a third of a pawn better], develops a knight and attacks the e4 pawn, which White must defend. The engine line shows the natural continuation: 4. Nc3 cxd4 5. Nxd4 a6 6. Bg5. Black keeps the c-pawn tension for a move, then trades on d4, and ...a6 prepares ...e6 for a solid setup.

Black should avoid 3...Nd7. After 4. dxc5 Nxc5, White gets a clearly better game, about a pawn ahead [+0.82], because Black's c5 pawn is lost or Black's pieces are tangled.

The other reasonable choice is 3...cxd4 [−0.30], nearly as good. It opens the c-file at once, and after 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6. Bg5 Black reaches a similar structure with a little less tension.

For the typical plans in this structure, see *Fundamental Chess Openings* by Paul van der Sterren (the Sicilian chapter), and *Pawn Structure Chess* by Andrew Soltis for the open Sicilian pawn families.
